final_text: November, December, and half of January passed. Christmas and New Year had been celebrated at Gateshead with the usual festivities—presents exchanged, dinners and parties given. I was excluded from all of it, of course. My share of the celebrations consisted of watching Eliza and Georgiana get dressed in their thin muslin frocks and red sashes, their hair elaborately curled, and seeing them go down to the drawing room. After that, I listened to the sounds of piano or harp playing below, to the footsteps of the butler and footman, to the clinking of glass and china as refreshments were served, and to the muffled hum of conversation whenever the drawing room door opened and closed. When I tired of this, I retreated from the top of the stairs to the lonely, silent nursery. There, though somewhat sad, I wasn't miserable. To tell the truth, I had no desire to join the company—when I was among people, I was almost never noticed. If Bessie had only been kind and companionable, I would have considered it a treat to spend the evenings quietly with her instead of enduring the formidable gaze of Mrs. Reed in a room full of guests. But as soon as Bessie had dressed the young ladies, she took herself off to the lively kitchen and housekeeper's room, usually taking the candle with her. I would sit with my doll on my knee until the fire burned low, glancing around now and then to make sure nothing worse than myself haunted the shadowy room. When the embers faded to a dull red, I undressed quickly, struggling with knots and strings as best I could, and sought shelter from the cold and darkness in my crib. I always took my doll to bed with me. Human beings need to love something, and with nothing worthier to love, I managed to find pleasure in loving and cherishing a faded graven image, shabby as a miniature scarecrow. It puzzles me now to remember with what absurd devotion I doted on this toy, half-imagining it was alive and could feel. I couldn't sleep unless it was tucked inside my nightgown, and when it lay there safe and warm, I was relatively happy, believing it was happy too.

When she was gentle like this, Bessie seemed to me the best, prettiest, kindest person in the world, and I desperately wished she would always be so pleasant and never push me around or scold me or make unreasonable demands, as she too often did.
